top_news.title: Chandigarh University Hosts National Incubator & Capital Summit and ISBACON 2026, Bringing 400 Incubators, 80 Investors & 100 Startups Together to Strengthen India
top_news.summary: Aimed at strengthening access to early-stage investment for startups by connecting India's incubation institutions with investors, industry and policymakers, Chandigarh University brought together more than 400 incubator institutions from more than 20 States and Union Territories, over 100 startups, 80 investors and more than 60 government, policy and industry delegates on a single platform at Incubator & Capital Summit 2026 and ISBACON 2026. Hosted by Chandigarh University Technology Business Incubator (CU-TBI) in collaboration with the Indian Science and Technology Entrepreneurs Parks and Business Incubators' Association (ISBA), the four-day mega summit brought together incubators, founders, investors, policymakers, industry leaders and academic institutions to expand collaboration around investment, co-incubation, research and industry partnerships, while connecting startups with mentors, capital, technology and market opportunities and enabling incubators to share cohorts, expertise and infrastructure for wider startup growth across India. To create a national platform for scaling startup innovation across India, Chandigarh University launched the Central Innovation & Incubation Hub (C-Hub) as an 'Incubator of Incubators' Consortium, inaugurated by Gaurav Gautam, Minister of State, Youth Empowerment & Entrepreneurship, Sports, Law & Legislative, Haryana along with Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha) and Chancellor Chandigarh University Satnam Singh Sandhu. The Hub will connect incubators and startup support institutions to facilitate shared cohorts, mentors, infrastructure and investor partnerships, while enabling startups to access wider incubation support, early-stage capital, industry connections and market opportunities across India. Among the prominent personalities who participated in the summit were Rikant Pitte, Founder & CEO EaseMyTrip, Yoav Fekete, Innovation Attache at Embassy of Israel, Prasad Menon, President, ISBA CEO, Centre for Incubation and Business Acceleration (CIBA), Raghavendra, Joint Secretary, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Shashank Randev, Founder, 247VC among others. Speaking on the occasion, Gaurav Gautam, Minister of State, Youth Empowerment & Entrepreneurship, Sports, Law & Legislative, Haryana, said, "Indian youth have the responsibility of realizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of a 'Viksit Bharat 2047' and make the nation lead the world across every sector, from startups and digital technology to incubators and new unicorns. India's youth should not fear failure and keep striving to move forward. One day, your startup idea will serve the nation, benefit India and bring success. India's youth should dream big as the nation is fully prepared today to give wings to their ideas." "Thanks to the talent of India's youth and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of providing them with new platforms, things have changed in the country after 2014. India is now creating its own technology and we are moving beyond merely importing goods to excelling across every sector. Before 2014, we hardly ever heard terms like 'Digital India' or 'startups', mobile penetration was minimal and more than half of this country's population was previously unconnected to the formal economy. Now though DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) funds reach the accounts of people living in areas without internet access and UPI is being used by the common man. All this transformation is driven by India's youth who are envisioning how to advance technology, champion new ideas and scale up startups. They are figuring out how to collaborate with incubators and engage with new investors, this is the spirit of India's youth," the minister added. Member of Parliament and Chandigarh University Chancellor Satnam Singh Sandhu, said, "The vision and resolve of Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a 'Viksit Bharat' is coming true. India's startup ecosystem and entrepreneurs will play the most significant part in transforming our country into a developed nation by 2047. India's growing startup ecosystem, with around 2.25 lakh startups and over 125 unicorns, reflects the country's entrepreneurial potential. However, the focus must now shift from increasing numbers to ensuring the quality, sustainability and global competitiveness of startups. Profitability is essential for the long-term sustainability of any venture. At the same time, strong leadership skills are equally important for both entrepreneurs and professionals to drive innovation and growth. Indian startups must focus on developing quality products and solutions that can compete globally and contribute meaningfully to the nation's journey towards becoming a developed country by 2047." Yoav Fekete, Innovation Attache at Embassy of Israel, said, "As Punjab's agricultural strengths provide foundation for creation of valuable new material, bio-based eco-responsible packaging can be made from agricultural residue. It can not only add income for farmers but also provide an alternative to single-use plastics packaging. Our long-standing agricultural cooperation offers the foundation for an Indian-Israeli partnership to develop new opportunities after the harvest. Indian and Israeli researchers, entrepreneurs, and industrial partners should come together to co-develop such technology for locally available agricultural residues in North India and creating packaging for Indian businesses. This is an environmental and business opportunity. A reliable market for agricultural residue can create additional source of income for farmers and opportunities for local enterprises." "The world is standing at the crossroads today where AI can deepen the divide between the poor and the rich and those who own the tools and those who are only bound for them. But AI is also providing extraordinary possibilities in health, agriculture, education, manufacturing, and in how we care for our planet. Researchers have the responsibility of choosing what to build, founders need to choose what to sell, and investors choosing what to fund," he added. Prasad Menon, President, ISBA, said, "It's early days for incubator movement in India. But given the diversity of India, it's not just about numbers of incubators in the country, but it's also about whether we have managed to reach and penetrate incubators across different states of India across different regions. I'm very proud to say that ISBA represents incubators from all across India and we attempt to ensure that all the voices, whether it is big or small, are heard. With all the development that India has seen over the years, startups can't have a growth unless the ecosystem also grows. The number of incubators in India may not have grown proportionally with startup ecosystem, but incubators play major role in putting the startups in the front. When it comes to incubation, there's nothing like one size fits all and diversity of our country needs diversity of incubator ecosystem." The summit brought together technology business incubators, Atal Incubation Centres, university innovation heads, IPR leaders, startup support institutions, investors, policymakers and corporate representatives from across the country. The summit was designed to facilitate collaboration between institutions that support startups at different stages, enable founders to access early-stage capital, create opportunities for co-incubation and corporate partnerships and develop stronger national innovation networks beyond the major startup centres. The C-HUB is designed to bring niche incubators and venture-support activities together through shared programmes, investor relations, partnerships and a common technology and data platform. Alongside C-Hub, the University announced a co-incubation framework under which partner incubators can work with CU-TBI through shared cohorts, mentors and infrastructure. Joint cohorts with venture capital firms were also announced, creating a structured channel through which participating funds can engage with CU-incubated ventures. Chandigarh University also signed MoUs with 100 leading incubators across India to establish joint cohorts and co-incubation programmes, enabling greater collaboration, shared expertise and resources to support startup growth and scale ventures nationwide. The summit featured focused discussions on entrepreneurship, networked incubation, deep-tech and startup financing. Rikant Pittie, Co-founder, EaseMyTrip, shared his journey from bootstrapping to public markets, while Raghavendra, Joint Secretary, DPIIT; Dr. Basant Garg, IAS, Administrative Secretary, Industries & Commerce and IT, Government of Punjab; Atul Kumar, Director, Data Security Council of India and P. J. Singh, CMD, Tynor Orthotics and Vice President, CII, discussed how policy, industry and regional hubs can strengthen startup outcomes. Dr. Panneerselvam Madanagopal, CEO, MeitY Startup Hub; Dr. K. Suresh Kumar, Executive Director, PSG-STEP and Dr. Praveen Roy, Scientist 'G' and Head, TTI Division, DST, explored deep-tech capabilities for incubators, while Dr. Dhananjay K. Tiwary, Managing Director, BIRAC; Jai Shah, Principal Investment Officer, NEEV Fund, SBI Ventures and Vipul Patel, Partner - Seed Investing, IIMA Ventures, discussed stronger financing pathways for startups and incubators. The Microsoft UNNATI AI 2.0 Roadshow brought together representatives from Microsoft, FITT-IIT Delhi, iHub, India Accelerator and TiE Delhi for discussions around AI and the startup ecosystem. The summit's four-day programme further includes the Startup Expo, incubator exchange, masterclasses, policy roundtables, investor meetings, Demo Day and industry engagement, providing multiple opportunities for startups and incubation institutions to move from introductions to concrete collaborations. Chandigarh University Maps 51 National Centres of Excellence for Collaboration CU-TBI has mapped 51 Centres of Excellence across India as potential collaborators, comprising 35 academic, 14 government, one industry-academia and one non-profit research institute. Hosted at institutions including IISc, IITs, IIM Ahmedabad, STPI, NIELIT, ICMR and CSIR, these centres span quantum technology, AI, robotics, chip design, healthcare, materials, defence and financial markets, opening avenues for research, technology collaboration and stronger support for innovation-driven startups. top_news.title: From Defence Cooperation to Shared Security: Building a Resilient Pakistan-China Partnership
top_news.summary: QINGDAO, China, Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A report fromIQINGDAO. Security is becoming a broader test of the Pakistan-China partnership. The threats facing both countries no longer fall neatly within the boundaries of conventional defence. Terrorism and cross-border militancy, attacks on personnel and strategic infrastructure, cyber threats and rapidly advancing military technologies are reshaping the security environment in which both countries operate. A news report from General Ehsan ul Haq Pakistan and China already possess a deeply institutionalised defence relationship, built through military exchanges, joint exercises, training, defence production and technology cooperation. That foundation has given the partnership considerable strategic depth. But the nature of the challenges now facing both countries requires this cooperation to evolve further-from defence cooperation towards shared security resilience. For Pakistan, this means strengthening the national capabilities, institutions and technologies needed to anticipate and respond to emerging threats. For China, the security and stability of Pakistan are directly connected to the safety of its citizens and interests in the country and to the stability of China's wider western neighbourhood. Both therefore have a strategic interest in building a security partnership that is more preventive, technologically capable and institutionally coordinated. The next phase should not be measured simply by the number of exercises conducted or systems acquired. Its real measure will be whether Pakistan and China can build the capabilities and coordination necessary to prevent threats, protect shared interests and sustain strategic stability in an increasingly complex security environment. The Security Environment Has Outgrown the TraditionalDefence Model Pakistan-China security cooperation was built around a conventional understanding of national security, shaped by the strategic environment of the second half of the twentieth century. That foundation remains important, but the risks facing both countries have become more interconnected. Terrorism, instability along borders, attacks on strategic infrastructure, cyber threats and vulnerabilities in critical systems can now affect national security without taking the form of conventional military conflict. For Pakistan, this has particular significance. Its security environment extends from the western frontier to major economic and infrastructure corridors, while the protection of Chinese personnel and projects has become an important dimension of bilateral security. For China, instability in Pakistan can affect the safety of its citizens, strategic interests and wider regional connectivity. The implication is that defence cooperation can no longer operate as a separate military track. Security increasingly depends on how effectively defence institutions, counterterrorism capabilities, technology and protection arrangements reinforce one another. The strategic task for Pakistan and China is therefore not simply to expand existing cooperation, but to adapt it to a security environment in which threats are increasingly interconnected, faster-moving and less predictable. Defence Cooperation Has Created a Foundation for National Capability The depth of Pakistan-China defence cooperation lies not simply in the systems the two countries have acquired or developed, but in the capabilities and institutions created around them. Military exchanges, joint exercises, training and defence production have progressively moved the relationship beyond conventional defence procurement towards a model of cooperation in which Pakistan participates in developing, producing and sustaining critical capabilities. The JF-17 Thunder is the clearest example. Its joint development and production created expertise in assembly, maintenance, technical support and sustainment within Pakistan. Its strategic value therefore extends beyond the platform itself. It demonstrates what becomes possible when defence cooperation is structured around the transfer of knowledge and the development of domestic capability rather than the delivery of finished equipment alone. That distinction will matter increasingly as modern security becomes more technologically demanding. Military effectiveness depends not only on platforms, but on the ability to maintain systems, integrate new technologies, develop specialised expertise and adapt capabilities as threats evolve. Defence cooperation is therefore most valuable when it leaves behind skills, institutions and industrial capacity that strengthen a country's ability to respond independently to future challenges. Pakistan and China should build on this experience. The next stage of cooperation should place greater emphasis, where appropriate, on joint research, technical training, maintenance, innovation and defence-industrial development. The objective should not simply be to expand Pakistan's defence inventory, but to deepen the national capabilities that enable it to sustain and continuously strengthen its security posture. From Incident Response to Preventive Security The most immediate test of Pakistan-China security cooperation is whether both countries can move from responding to individual attacks towards preventing threats before they materialise. Repeated attacks against Chinese nationals and projects in Pakistan demonstrate that terrorism is not simply a domestic security challenge; it has become a vulnerability within the strategic relationship itself. Pakistan's response to these threats has already involved established security arrangements and sustained efforts by its security institutions to protect Chinese personnel and CPEC projects. Pakistani security personnel have also lost their lives in carrying out this responsibility, underscoring the seriousness of the commitment and the human cost involved. These efforts provide an important operational foundation for the next stage of Pakistan-China security cooperation. Pakistan and China already have established mechanisms for counterterrorism and security cooperation. In May 2026, the two sides agreed to establish a China-Pakistan Security Partnership and to strengthen bilateral and multilateral counterterrorism cooperation. They also reaffirmed the need to prevent terrorist groups, including the TTP and ETIM, from using territory to threaten regional security. The challenge, therefore, is not the absence of cooperation but how effectively existing mechanisms convert information into prevention. A stronger security architecture would connect intelligence collection, threat assessment, early warning and operational response more systematically. The objective should be to identify patterns and indicators of an emerging threat early enough for preventive measures to be taken, rather than relying primarily on heightened security after an incident has occurred. This requires closer coordination in assessing threats to Chinese personnel and strategic interests, developing common risk assessments and strengthening mechanisms through which relevant intelligence can inform protective decisions. Security incidents should also generate structured assessments of what failed, what warning indicators were missed and how protective measures should subsequently change. Such an approach would turn individual incidents into institutional learning rather than treating each attack as a separate security episode. The regional dimension cannot be ignored. Instability in Afghanistan and along Pakistan's western frontier can provide militant networks with space to organise, move and operate. Pakistan and China therefore have a shared interest in improving their understanding of cross-border threats and using appropriate regional channels to address them. The objective should be a shift from reaction to prevention. A resilient security partnership is one in which intelligence leads to assessment, assessment leads to timely action, and each security incident strengthens the system's ability to prevent the next one. Security Technology Must Become a Capability, Not a Commodity The next stage of Pakistan-China defence cooperation should focus not only on acquiring advanced technology, but on building the capacity to adapt and sustain it. As security becomes increasingly technology-driven, strategic advantage depends on the ability to integrate new systems, develop specialised expertise and adapt capabilities as threats evolve. Pakistan-China cooperation already provides a foundation for this approach through joint defence production and technical cooperation. The JF-17 experience demonstrates the value of moving beyond finished equipment towards shared expertise and industrial capability. The same principle can guide cooperation in emerging areas such as cybersecurity, unmanned systems, secure communications and electronic warfare. Rather than pursuing technology for its own sake, both countries should identify specific security requirements where joint research, technical training and system integration can produce lasting capability. For Pakistan, this means using cooperation to strengthen domestic expertise and institutional capacity. For China, it means developing a more capable and resilient security partner. The strategic objective is technological capability: ensuring that both countries can absorb new technologies, adapt them to changing security requirements and sustain critical capabilities over time. Protecting Strategic Interests Requires Stronger Institutional Resilience The security of Chinese personnel, projects and institutions in Pakistan has become a measure of confidence in the wider partnership. Pakistan has taken significant steps to strengthen protection arrangements, with Pakistani security personnel carrying out this responsibility at considerable risk and, in some cases, making the ultimate sacrifice while protecting Chinese citizens and CPEC projects. But repeated attacks demonstrate that physical security alone cannot address the full nature of the threat. The challenge is increasingly one of institutional resilience: the ability of security institutions to anticipate risks, coordinate across jurisdictions and sustain protection as threats evolve. This requires security planning to move beyond project-by-project arrangements towards a more integrated assessment of the environments in which Chinese personnel and strategic interests operate. Threat patterns, local conditions and emerging risks should inform security planning before vulnerabilities become incidents. For Pakistan, this is fundamentally a national security responsibility. For China, the security of its citizens and investments is directly connected to confidence in the country's ability to sustain long-term cooperation. Both interests therefore point towards the same objective: security arrangements that become more predictive, coordinated and adaptable over time. Building on the security arrangements and operational experience already developed, the next stage can place greater emphasis on preventive, intelligence-led and technology-enabled mechanisms. The measure of progress should be whether Pakistan's security system becomes increasingly capable of preventing threats rather than simply responding to them. That would strengthen not only the protection of Chinese interests, but the institutional foundations of the Pakistan-China partnership itself. The Next Step Is a More Integrated Security Partnership Pakistan and China do not need to build their security relationship from the ground up. They already have established channels for defence cooperation, counterterrorism, technology and the protection of Chinese personnel and strategic projects. The priority now should be to connect these areas more effectively. A practical step would be to establish a regular process for reviewing emerging security requirements across these fields and identifying where existing cooperation can be better aligned. Defence institutions, security agencies and technical experts could use such assessments to identify shared priorities, whether in counterterrorism, technological capability, professional training or protection arrangements. This would also create a clearer link between operational experience and future cooperation. Threats identified through security assessments could inform training and technology priorities, while lessons from operations could be incorporated into subsequent planning. The purpose is not another institution or another layer of agreements. It is better strategic alignment among the cooperation mechanisms already in place, allowing each to reinforce the others and ensuring that bilateral security cooperation evolves in response to actual requirements. Building Security That Can Sustain the Partnership Pakistan-China security cooperation has already developed substantial depth. The next challenge is to ensure that this cooperation produces capabilities that can withstand changing threats, technologies and geopolitical conditions. For Pakistan, this means strengthening the institutions and expertise that underpin national security. For China, it means a more capable partner able to protect shared interests and contribute to regional stability. The future strength of the partnership will not be measured simply by the systems acquired or agreements signed, but by the capabilities built through them. The next phase should therefore be defined by greater prevention, stronger capacity and the ability of both countries to adapt together.

articles.title: Chandigarh University Hosts National Incubator & Capital Summit and ISBACON 2026, Bringing 400 Incubators, 80 Investors & 100 Startups Together to Strengthen India
articles.summary: Aimed at strengthening access to early-stage investment for startups by connecting India's incubation institutions with investors, industry and policymakers, Chandigarh University brought together more than 400 incubator institutions from more than 20 States and Union Territories, over 100 startups, 80 investors and more than 60 government, policy and industry delegates on a single platform at Incubator & Capital Summit 2026 and ISBACON 2026. Hosted by Chandigarh University Technology Business Incubator (CU-TBI) in collaboration with the Indian Science and Technology Entrepreneurs Parks and Business Incubators' Association (ISBA), the four-day mega summit brought together incubators, founders, investors, policymakers, industry leaders and academic institutions to expand collaboration around investment, co-incubation, research and industry partnerships, while connecting startups with mentors, capital, technology and market opportunities and enabling incubators to share cohorts, expertise and infrastructure for wider startup growth across India. To create a national platform for scaling startup innovation across India, Chandigarh University launched the Central Innovation & Incubation Hub (C-Hub) as an 'Incubator of Incubators' Consortium, inaugurated by Gaurav Gautam, Minister of State, Youth Empowerment & Entrepreneurship, Sports, Law & Legislative, Haryana along with Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha) and Chancellor Chandigarh University Satnam Singh Sandhu. The Hub will connect incubators and startup support institutions to facilitate shared cohorts, mentors, infrastructure and investor partnerships, while enabling startups to access wider incubation support, early-stage capital, industry connections and market opportunities across India. Among the prominent personalities who participated in the summit were Rikant Pitte, Founder & CEO EaseMyTrip, Yoav Fekete, Innovation Attache at Embassy of Israel, Prasad Menon, President, ISBA CEO, Centre for Incubation and Business Acceleration (CIBA), Raghavendra, Joint Secretary, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Shashank Randev, Founder, 247VC among others. Speaking on the occasion, Gaurav Gautam, Minister of State, Youth Empowerment & Entrepreneurship, Sports, Law & Legislative, Haryana, said, "Indian youth have the responsibility of realizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of a 'Viksit Bharat 2047' and make the nation lead the world across every sector, from startups and digital technology to incubators and new unicorns. India's youth should not fear failure and keep striving to move forward. One day, your startup idea will serve the nation, benefit India and bring success. India's youth should dream big as the nation is fully prepared today to give wings to their ideas." "Thanks to the talent of India's youth and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of providing them with new platforms, things have changed in the country after 2014. India is now creating its own technology and we are moving beyond merely importing goods to excelling across every sector. Before 2014, we hardly ever heard terms like 'Digital India' or 'startups', mobile penetration was minimal and more than half of this country's population was previously unconnected to the formal economy. Now though DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) funds reach the accounts of people living in areas without internet access and UPI is being used by the common man. All this transformation is driven by India's youth who are envisioning how to advance technology, champion new ideas and scale up startups. They are figuring out how to collaborate with incubators and engage with new investors, this is the spirit of India's youth," the minister added. Member of Parliament and Chandigarh University Chancellor Satnam Singh Sandhu, said, "The vision and resolve of Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a 'Viksit Bharat' is coming true. India's startup ecosystem and entrepreneurs will play the most significant part in transforming our country into a developed nation by 2047. India's growing startup ecosystem, with around 2.25 lakh startups and over 125 unicorns, reflects the country's entrepreneurial potential. However, the focus must now shift from increasing numbers to ensuring the quality, sustainability and global competitiveness of startups. Profitability is essential for the long-term sustainability of any venture. At the same time, strong leadership skills are equally important for both entrepreneurs and professionals to drive innovation and growth. Indian startups must focus on developing quality products and solutions that can compete globally and contribute meaningfully to the nation's journey towards becoming a developed country by 2047." Yoav Fekete, Innovation Attache at Embassy of Israel, said, "As Punjab's agricultural strengths provide foundation for creation of valuable new material, bio-based eco-responsible packaging can be made from agricultural residue. It can not only add income for farmers but also provide an alternative to single-use plastics packaging. Our long-standing agricultural cooperation offers the foundation for an Indian-Israeli partnership to develop new opportunities after the harvest. Indian and Israeli researchers, entrepreneurs, and industrial partners should come together to co-develop such technology for locally available agricultural residues in North India and creating packaging for Indian businesses. This is an environmental and business opportunity. A reliable market for agricultural residue can create additional source of income for farmers and opportunities for local enterprises." "The world is standing at the crossroads today where AI can deepen the divide between the poor and the rich and those who own the tools and those who are only bound for them. But AI is also providing extraordinary possibilities in health, agriculture, education, manufacturing, and in how we care for our planet. Researchers have the responsibility of choosing what to build, founders need to choose what to sell, and investors choosing what to fund," he added. Prasad Menon, President, ISBA, said, "It's early days for incubator movement in India. But given the diversity of India, it's not just about numbers of incubators in the country, but it's also about whether we have managed to reach and penetrate incubators across different states of India across different regions. I'm very proud to say that ISBA represents incubators from all across India and we attempt to ensure that all the voices, whether it is big or small, are heard. With all the development that India has seen over the years, startups can't have a growth unless the ecosystem also grows. The number of incubators in India may not have grown proportionally with startup ecosystem, but incubators play major role in putting the startups in the front. When it comes to incubation, there's nothing like one size fits all and diversity of our country needs diversity of incubator ecosystem." The summit brought together technology business incubators, Atal Incubation Centres, university innovation heads, IPR leaders, startup support institutions, investors, policymakers and corporate representatives from across the country. The summit was designed to facilitate collaboration between institutions that support startups at different stages, enable founders to access early-stage capital, create opportunities for co-incubation and corporate partnerships and develop stronger national innovation networks beyond the major startup centres. The C-HUB is designed to bring niche incubators and venture-support activities together through shared programmes, investor relations, partnerships and a common technology and data platform. Alongside C-Hub, the University announced a co-incubation framework under which partner incubators can work with CU-TBI through shared cohorts, mentors and infrastructure. Joint cohorts with venture capital firms were also announced, creating a structured channel through which participating funds can engage with CU-incubated ventures. Chandigarh University also signed MoUs with 100 leading incubators across India to establish joint cohorts and co-incubation programmes, enabling greater collaboration, shared expertise and resources to support startup growth and scale ventures nationwide. The summit featured focused discussions on entrepreneurship, networked incubation, deep-tech and startup financing. Rikant Pittie, Co-founder, EaseMyTrip, shared his journey from bootstrapping to public markets, while Raghavendra, Joint Secretary, DPIIT; Dr. Basant Garg, IAS, Administrative Secretary, Industries & Commerce and IT, Government of Punjab; Atul Kumar, Director, Data Security Council of India and P. J. Singh, CMD, Tynor Orthotics and Vice President, CII, discussed how policy, industry and regional hubs can strengthen startup outcomes. Dr. Panneerselvam Madanagopal, CEO, MeitY Startup Hub; Dr. K. Suresh Kumar, Executive Director, PSG-STEP and Dr. Praveen Roy, Scientist 'G' and Head, TTI Division, DST, explored deep-tech capabilities for incubators, while Dr. Dhananjay K. Tiwary, Managing Director, BIRAC; Jai Shah, Principal Investment Officer, NEEV Fund, SBI Ventures and Vipul Patel, Partner - Seed Investing, IIMA Ventures, discussed stronger financing pathways for startups and incubators. The Microsoft UNNATI AI 2.0 Roadshow brought together representatives from Microsoft, FITT-IIT Delhi, iHub, India Accelerator and TiE Delhi for discussions around AI and the startup ecosystem. The summit's four-day programme further includes the Startup Expo, incubator exchange, masterclasses, policy roundtables, investor meetings, Demo Day and industry engagement, providing multiple opportunities for startups and incubation institutions to move from introductions to concrete collaborations. Chandigarh University Maps 51 National Centres of Excellence for Collaboration CU-TBI has mapped 51 Centres of Excellence across India as potential collaborators, comprising 35 academic, 14 government, one industry-academia and one non-profit research institute. Hosted at institutions including IISc, IITs, IIM Ahmedabad, STPI, NIELIT, ICMR and CSIR, these centres span quantum technology, AI, robotics, chip design, healthcare, materials, defence and financial markets, opening avenues for research, technology collaboration and stronger support for innovation-driven startups. About Chandigarh University Chandigarh University is a NAAC A+ Grade University and QS World Ranked University. This autonomous educational institution is approved by UGC and is located near Chandigarh in the state of Punjab. It is the youngest university in India and the only private university in Punjab to be honoured with A+ Grade by NAAC (National Assessment and Accreditation Council). CU offers more than 109 UG and PG programs in the field of engineering, management, pharmacy, law, architecture, journalism, animation, hotel management, commerce, and others. articles.title: From Defence Cooperation to Shared Security: Building a Resilient Pakistan-China Partnership
articles.summary: QINGDAO, China, Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A report fromIQINGDAO. Security is becoming a broader test of the Pakistan-China partnership. The threats facing both countries no longer fall neatly within the boundaries of conventional defence. Terrorism and cross-border militancy, attacks on personnel and strategic infrastructure, cyber threats and rapidly advancing military technologies are reshaping the security environment in which both countries operate. A news report from General Ehsan ul Haq Pakistan and China already possess a deeply institutionalised defence relationship, built through military exchanges, joint exercises, training, defence production and technology cooperation. That foundation has given the partnership considerable strategic depth. But the nature of the challenges now facing both countries requires this cooperation to evolve further-from defence cooperation towards shared security resilience. For Pakistan, this means strengthening the national capabilities, institutions and technologies needed to anticipate and respond to emerging threats. For China, the security and stability of Pakistan are directly connected to the safety of its citizens and interests in the country and to the stability of China's wider western neighbourhood. Both therefore have a strategic interest in building a security partnership that is more preventive, technologically capable and institutionally coordinated. The next phase should not be measured simply by the number of exercises conducted or systems acquired. Its real measure will be whether Pakistan and China can build the capabilities and coordination necessary to prevent threats, protect shared interests and sustain strategic stability in an increasingly complex security environment. The Security Environment Has Outgrown the TraditionalDefence Model Pakistan-China security cooperation was built around a conventional understanding of national security, shaped by the strategic environment of the second half of the twentieth century. That foundation remains important, but the risks facing both countries have become more interconnected. Terrorism, instability along borders, attacks on strategic infrastructure, cyber threats and vulnerabilities in critical systems can now affect national security without taking the form of conventional military conflict. For Pakistan, this has particular significance. Its security environment extends from the western frontier to major economic and infrastructure corridors, while the protection of Chinese personnel and projects has become an important dimension of bilateral security. For China, instability in Pakistan can affect the safety of its citizens, strategic interests and wider regional connectivity. The implication is that defence cooperation can no longer operate as a separate military track. Security increasingly depends on how effectively defence institutions, counterterrorism capabilities, technology and protection arrangements reinforce one another. The strategic task for Pakistan and China is therefore not simply to expand existing cooperation, but to adapt it to a security environment in which threats are increasingly interconnected, faster-moving and less predictable. Defence Cooperation Has Created a Foundation for National Capability The depth of Pakistan-China defence cooperation lies not simply in the systems the two countries have acquired or developed, but in the capabilities and institutions created around them. Military exchanges, joint exercises, training and defence production have progressively moved the relationship beyond conventional defence procurement towards a model of cooperation in which Pakistan participates in developing, producing and sustaining critical capabilities. The JF-17 Thunder is the clearest example. Its joint development and production created expertise in assembly, maintenance, technical support and sustainment within Pakistan. Its strategic value therefore extends beyond the platform itself. It demonstrates what becomes possible when defence cooperation is structured around the transfer of knowledge and the development of domestic capability rather than the delivery of finished equipment alone. That distinction will matter increasingly as modern security becomes more technologically demanding. Military effectiveness depends not only on platforms, but on the ability to maintain systems, integrate new technologies, develop specialised expertise and adapt capabilities as threats evolve. Defence cooperation is therefore most valuable when it leaves behind skills, institutions and industrial capacity that strengthen a country's ability to respond independently to future challenges. Pakistan and China should build on this experience. The next stage of cooperation should place greater emphasis, where appropriate, on joint research, technical training, maintenance, innovation and defence-industrial development. The objective should not simply be to expand Pakistan's defence inventory, but to deepen the national capabilities that enable it to sustain and continuously strengthen its security posture. From Incident Response to Preventive Security The most immediate test of Pakistan-China security cooperation is whether both countries can move from responding to individual attacks towards preventing threats before they materialise. Repeated attacks against Chinese nationals and projects in Pakistan demonstrate that terrorism is not simply a domestic security challenge; it has become a vulnerability within the strategic relationship itself. Pakistan's response to these threats has already involved established security arrangements and sustained efforts by its security institutions to protect Chinese personnel and CPEC projects. Pakistani security personnel have also lost their lives in carrying out this responsibility, underscoring the seriousness of the commitment and the human cost involved. These efforts provide an important operational foundation for the next stage of Pakistan-China security cooperation. Pakistan and China already have established mechanisms for counterterrorism and security cooperation. In May 2026, the two sides agreed to establish a China-Pakistan Security Partnership and to strengthen bilateral and multilateral counterterrorism cooperation. They also reaffirmed the need to prevent terrorist groups, including the TTP and ETIM, from using territory to threaten regional security. The challenge, therefore, is not the absence of cooperation but how effectively existing mechanisms convert information into prevention. A stronger security architecture would connect intelligence collection, threat assessment, early warning and operational response more systematically. The objective should be to identify patterns and indicators of an emerging threat early enough for preventive measures to be taken, rather than relying primarily on heightened security after an incident has occurred. This requires closer coordination in assessing threats to Chinese personnel and strategic interests, developing common risk assessments and strengthening mechanisms through which relevant intelligence can inform protective decisions. Security incidents should also generate structured assessments of what failed, what warning indicators were missed and how protective measures should subsequently change. Such an approach would turn individual incidents into institutional learning rather than treating each attack as a separate security episode. The regional dimension cannot be ignored. Instability in Afghanistan and along Pakistan's western frontier can provide militant networks with space to organise, move and operate. Pakistan and China therefore have a shared interest in improving their understanding of cross-border threats and using appropriate regional channels to address them. The objective should be a shift from reaction to prevention. A resilient security partnership is one in which intelligence leads to assessment, assessment leads to timely action, and each security incident strengthens the system's ability to prevent the next one. Security Technology Must Become a Capability, Not a Commodity The next stage of Pakistan-China defence cooperation should focus not only on acquiring advanced technology, but on building the capacity to adapt and sustain it. As security becomes increasingly technology-driven, strategic advantage depends on the ability to integrate new systems, develop specialised expertise and adapt capabilities as threats evolve. Pakistan-China cooperation already provides a foundation for this approach through joint defence production and technical cooperation. The JF-17 experience demonstrates the value of moving beyond finished equipment towards shared expertise and industrial capability. The same principle can guide cooperation in emerging areas such as cybersecurity, unmanned systems, secure communications and electronic warfare. Rather than pursuing technology for its own sake, both countries should identify specific security requirements where joint research, technical training and system integration can produce lasting capability. For Pakistan, this means using cooperation to strengthen domestic expertise and institutional capacity. For China, it means developing a more capable and resilient security partner. The strategic objective is technological capability: ensuring that both countries can absorb new technologies, adapt them to changing security requirements and sustain critical capabilities over time. Protecting Strategic Interests Requires Stronger Institutional Resilience The security of Chinese personnel, projects and institutions in Pakistan has become a measure of confidence in the wider partnership. Pakistan has taken significant steps to strengthen protection arrangements, with Pakistani security personnel carrying out this responsibility at considerable risk and, in some cases, making the ultimate sacrifice while protecting Chinese citizens and CPEC projects. But repeated attacks demonstrate that physical security alone cannot address the full nature of the threat. The challenge is increasingly one of institutional resilience: the ability of security institutions to anticipate risks, coordinate across jurisdictions and sustain protection as threats evolve. This requires security planning to move beyond project-by-project arrangements towards a more integrated assessment of the environments in which Chinese personnel and strategic interests operate. Threat patterns, local conditions and emerging risks should inform security planning before vulnerabilities become incidents. For Pakistan, this is fundamentally a national security responsibility. For China, the security of its citizens and investments is directly connected to confidence in the country's ability to sustain long-term cooperation. Both interests therefore point towards the same objective: security arrangements that become more predictive, coordinated and adaptable over time. Building on the security arrangements and operational experience already developed, the next stage can place greater emphasis on preventive, intelligence-led and technology-enabled mechanisms. The measure of progress should be whether Pakistan's security system becomes increasingly capable of preventing threats rather than simply responding to them. That would strengthen not only the protection of Chinese interests, but the institutional foundations of the Pakistan-China partnership itself. The Next Step Is a More Integrated Security Partnership Pakistan and China do not need to build their security relationship from the ground up. They already have established channels for defence cooperation, counterterrorism, technology and the protection of Chinese personnel and strategic projects. The priority now should be to connect these areas more effectively. A practical step would be to establish a regular process for reviewing emerging security requirements across these fields and identifying where existing cooperation can be better aligned. Defence institutions, security agencies and technical experts could use such assessments to identify shared priorities, whether in counterterrorism, technological capability, professional training or protection arrangements. This would also create a clearer link between operational experience and future cooperation. Threats identified through security assessments could inform training and technology priorities, while lessons from operations could be incorporated into subsequent planning. The purpose is not another institution or another layer of agreements. It is better strategic alignment among the cooperation mechanisms already in place, allowing each to reinforce the others and ensuring that bilateral security cooperation evolves in response to actual requirements. Building Security That Can Sustain the Partnership Pakistan-China security cooperation has already developed substantial depth. The next challenge is to ensure that this cooperation produces capabilities that can withstand changing threats, technologies and geopolitical conditions. For Pakistan, this means strengthening the institutions and expertise that underpin national security. For China, it means a more capable partner able to protect shared interests and contribute to regional stability. The future strength of the partnership will not be measured simply by the systems acquired or agreements signed, but by the capabilities built through them. The next phase should therefore be defined by greater prevention, stronger capacity and the ability of both countries to adapt together.
